events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks from its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens. Identify what evidence would justify each choice.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intent assumed; Test budget EUR 20000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget: 7 searches left; one challenge_theory allowed; Financial data only partly public; state what cannot be reconciled; Must establish how far RATIONAL already reaches individual buyers before assuming anything. Alternatives: A. No expansion: deepen the professional core (service, installed base, chef training, financing); B. Premium home product: a smaller, consumer-priced combi-steamer sold direct to home cooks; C. Indirect route: license or co-brand the technology with existing home appliance makers, RATIONAL as technology supplier; D. Adjacent professional customer: scaled-down units for small restaurants, caterers, bakeries or ghost kitchens; E. Consumer content, accessory or retail-channel route: training, recipes, accessories, or a consumer version sold through existing retail or online platforms without a new brand; F. Defer: monitor the home-cooking market and wait for competitor or customer signals before committing capital.
Searched for "RATIONAL home cooking consumer product"; found rational-anova-oven, rational-ir-customers, rational-ir-leader.

T1: Enthusiast home cooks would pay a premium for a compact combi-steamer that carries the performance reputation of professional units, because they already buy premium countertop appliances and value professional-grade results. A maker that controls the technology and brand could capture that premium. Who benefits: Affluent enthusiast home cooks, and RATIONAL if it captures a premium price on a smaller unit sold direct or through a licensee.. Why behaviour changes: A professional brand is a credible quality signal. Buyers who already pay for precision cookers and countertop ovens may trade up if the product clearly delivers restaurant results at home.. How value is captured: A consumer-priced premium appliance, either sold direct under the RATIONAL brand or licensed to an appliance maker that pays a royalty on the technology.. Assumptions: A meaningful enthusiast segment exists that will pay a premium for a combi-steamer; A smaller unit can keep the performance that makes the brand credible; RATIONAL can sell to consumers without damaging its commercial brand or channel relationships. Predictions: Consumer price tests above a typical premium countertop oven show purchase intent among enthusiasts; Purchase intent falls sharply when the brand is removed from the message; Competitor countertop combi ovens sell in enough volume to show a real segment.

T2: Home cooks do not value a professional combi-steamer's performance enough to pay for it. The commercial value of RATIONAL lies in its installed base, service network and financing for professional kitchens, where switching costs are high. Entering the home market would dilute the brand and divert capital, so the best return comes from deepening the professional core. Who benefits: RATIONAL's existing professional customers and shareholders, who keep a focused franchise with recurring service revenue.. Why behaviour changes: Professional buyers stay because service uptime, training and HACCP-style hygiene support matter to their business. Home buyers have no such need, so the professional advantage does not transfer to the home.. How value is captured: Installed-base service contracts, consumables, chef training and financing in the commercial market, with no consumer product.. Assumptions: Switching costs and service value are the main reasons professional kitchens buy from RATIONAL; Home cooks do not treat a commercial brand as a reason to pay more; Capital spent on a consumer product would earn less than the commercial core. Predictions: Home-cooker purchase intent for a RATIONAL-branded appliance is low even at a moderate premium; Professional customer retention and service revenue hold up if the company stays focused; Competitors that tried consumer combi-steamers have not gained professional share.

T1 supports, from rational-anova-oven (market_fact): "the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods". Does not show: This shows only that a competitor sold a countertop combi oven for home use. It does not show sales volume, the price premium buyers paid, whether enthusiasts would pay more for a RATIONAL-branded unit, or whether the product succeeded. It is about Anova, not RATIONAL, and the source is an encyclopedia entry with no date..

T2 supports, from rational-ir-customers (company_assertion): "The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.". Does not show: This is the company's own description of its customers. It lists no consumer or home-cook buyers, but it does not give revenue shares, service contract values, retention rates or margins by segment, so it cannot show that the professional core is more profitable than a consumer product would be. It also does not show that home cooks would not buy..
Looked for evidence against T1: "consumer countertop combi steamer oven sales failure home cooks not buying"; found rational-combi-countertop, rational-anova-oven, rational-wiki-icombi90.

T1 neutral, from rational-combi-countertop (market_fact): "These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.". Does not show: This is a general encyclopedia statement about countertop combi appliances. It does not say whether the category sells, at what premium, or to whom. It says the category is cheaper than full-size ovens, which does not fit a premium-price claim well but does not show failure either. It gives no geography and no date, so it cannot show home demand in any market..

Test "Brand-blind and brand-named purchase-intent test for a compact combi-steamer" between T1; T2. Method: Online randomised concept test. Enthusiast home cooks are shown a compact countertop combi-steamer concept at a range of price points. Half see it with the RATIONAL brand and professional-performance claims, half see it with a neutral brand and the same specification. Stated purchase intent is followed by a refundable pre-order deposit on a subset, to check that intent converts to a commitment. The test is run through paid social and a recruited panel. Costs and sample sizes are proposed estimates, not observed figures.. Sample: Proposed: about 1200 respondents recruited from adults who own at least one premium countertop appliance and cook at home at least weekly, split across arms and price points. Pre-order arm of about 150 respondents.. Measure: Stated purchase intent at each price point, the difference in intent between branded and brand-blind arms, and conversion of intent to a refundable deposit.. Predictions: T1: The branded arm shows materially higher intent than the brand-blind arm at premium prices, and some enthusiasts convert to deposits at a premium price point.; T2: Intent is low in both arms, the branded advantage is small or absent, and deposits are negligible at any price point above a standard premium countertop oven.. Decision rule: Proceed with a consumer proposition only if at least 8 percent of the qualified panel shows intent at a premium price, the branded arm beats the brand-blind arm by at least 5 percentage points, and at least 3 percent of the pre-order arm places a deposit. Otherwise stop the consumer route and keep the professional core. Thresholds are proposed, not evidence-based.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.
Looked for evidence against T2: "RATIONAL professional installed base service revenue margin consumer segment"; found rational-ir-customers, rational-combi-household, rational-ir-figures.

T2 supports, from rational-ir-figures (company_assertion): "key figures from 2024: 50% global market share, sales of EUR 1,194 million, EBIT of EUR 314 million, EBIT margin of 26%, equity ratio of 77%, dividend payout ratio of 68%.". Does not show: These are the company's own group-level figures. They give no split between professional and any consumer activity, no service revenue, and no retention data, so they cannot show that the professional core earns more than a consumer product would. High group margins are consistent with T2 but do not prove that the cause is switching costs rather than product, price or brand. I could not check these figures against an independent filing in this investigation..

Favours T2: Do not build a home-cook product on the evidence so far. Keep the professional core as the default, and run the low-cost purchase-intent test (X1) before any consumer commitment. The evidence is thin on both sides: the sources show that RATIONAL's stated base is commercial and that group margins are high, and they show that a competitor sells a countertop combi oven for home use. None of them shows RATIONAL-branded consumer demand, pricing or retention, so T1 is untested rather than refuted. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T2 kept: The simulated warehouse label-printer result (SYN-D) measured nothing about buyers or wearers of cooking products, so even if it were real it would change nothing here. T2 is kept at its current uncertain rating on the company's own customer and figures claims, which show a commercial base but do not test consumer demand. SYN-D is not cited. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-ir-customers; rational-ir-figures.

T1 kept: Suppose SYN-D were real. It is a warehouse label-printer test that measured packing errors, not buyers, wearers or consumer willingness to pay. It bears on neither T1 nor T2, so even as a what-if it changes nothing. T1 stays uncertain. SYN-D is not cited as evidence in the finish. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not build a home-cook product on the current evidence. Keep the professional core as the default. Before any consumer commitment, run the proposed purchase-intent test (X1, proposed EUR 18,000 over about 10 weeks, within the EUR 20,000 and 12-week assumptions). The test has not been run. Neither the professional-core case nor the consumer case is established by what I could read. Target customer: No home-cook target is justified yet. If the test passes, the candidate is enthusiast home cooks who already buy premium countertop appliances.. Value proposition: Not established. The only candidate is a compact combi-steamer that carries the professional brand's performance credibility, priced above premium countertop ovens. Its premium is untested.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Approve and run test X1 with a brand-blind and a branded arm, using the proposed thresholds: at least 8 percent intent at a premium price, at least 5 percentage points brand lift, and at least 3 percent deposit conversion. Until then, keep the professional core and commit no capital to a consumer product. Request segment revenue and service data before relying on T2.. Uncertainty: High. RATIONAL's customer list, leadership claim, 50% market share and 2024 figures are company assertions I could not check against an independent filing. The sources show no split between professional and any consumer activity, and no service revenue or retention data, so T2's cause (switching costs and service value) is inferred, not measured. The one consumer-appliance source is about Anova, a different company, and gives no sales volume or price premium. Neither T1 nor T2 has been tested. The simulated warehouse result (SYN-D) was not used as evidence.. Would change if: Test X1 meets all three thresholds: at least 8 percent intent at a premium price, at least 5 percentage points brand lift over the brand-blind arm, and at least 3 percent deposit conversion. This would move T1 toward likely.; Independent sales data show that home combi-steamers or countertop combi ovens sell in meaningful volume at a premium price.; Segment or filing data show that professional service and installed-base revenue is small or shrinking, which would weaken T2.; Competitor evidence shows that consumer combi products tied to a professional brand failed to gain professional share, which would support T2 further.; Brand-blind intent matches branded intent, which would show the RATIONAL name adds nothing and weaken T1.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Simonelli Group develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing professional espresso-equipment offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked this question and nothing here reflects its intentions; Financial data may be incomplete; state what could not be found; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget: 8 total, 7 remaining; No SIMULATED results may be cited as evidence. Alternatives: No expansion: remain professional-only, focused on commercial cafe and foodservice buyers; Product redesign: adapt existing Nuova Simonelli or Victoria Arduino machines for home or prosumer use (smaller, simpler, lower price); Different route to buyers: sell existing prosumer machines through retailers, e-commerce or distributors, with no new product line; Different customer group: a distinct home or small-office branded line; Licensing or white-label partnership with a consumer appliance maker, keeping Simonelli's brand in professional; Adjacent accessory play: grinders or maintenance products sold to existing home-machine owners, without a full machine.

T1: Prosumers pay a premium for commercial-grade components and brand credibility, so a Simonelli home line sold on that heritage (e.g., the Oscar Mood's commercial-derived parts) could earn premium prices without a new product category. Who benefits: Enthusiast home buyers who want commercial-level performance and are willing to pay more for it; Simonelli, which already has the components and brand.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers treat a professional pedigree as proof of quality and durability, so they shift spend from mass-market appliances to a machine with a commercial heritage.. How value is captured: Price premium over mass-market home machines, sold through the existing Nuova Simonelli or Victoria Arduino brands, with margin protected by reusing commercial components.. Assumptions: Prosumer buyers will pay a meaningful premium for commercial heritage over mass-market home brands; Existing components can be reused at home-machine scale without redesign costs eroding margin; Simonelli's brand carries credibility outside the cafe trade. Predictions: Prosumer buyers in a survey or store test rate commercial pedigree as a top purchase reason; Price elasticity is low enough that a 20-40% premium over comparable home machines holds conversion; Sales concentrate among existing cafe-adjacent enthusiasts rather than mass retail.

T2: In prosumer espresso, value is captured by whoever controls consumer marketing and retail reach, not by the machine's commercial pedigree. Simonelli would earn more by partnering with or acquiring a consumer-channel player than by building its own home line. Who benefits: A consumer appliance group with retail and marketing reach (e.g., Breville, which bought Lelit), and a manufacturer like Simonelli that licenses or sells through them.. Why behaviour changes: Home buyers choose by brand familiarity, retail availability and reviews; a professional pedigree does not reach them without consumer marketing and shelf presence.. How value is captured: Acquisition or licensing that gives access to an established consumer brand, distribution and marketing, with Simonelli supplying the engineering and components.. Assumptions: Consumer appliance groups are willing to buy or license prosumer espresso brands at a premium; Consumer reach matters more than product pedigree for purchase decisions; Simonelli's professional business is not harmed by a consumer partner's brand. Predictions: Acquisitions in prosumer espresso are driven by a buyer's distribution and marketing, not by production capacity; Brands with weak consumer reach but strong pedigree sell fewer units in retail tests than brands with strong marketing and similar specs; Simonelli would sell through partners rather than own a consumer brand, with deal value tied to channel access.

T1 supports, from simo-dcn-oscar-mood-2021 (market_fact): "The original Nuova Simonelli Oscar, which introduced some of Nuova Simonelli’s high-quality and high-powered components to high-end home and prosumer audiences.". Does not show: Whether buyers pay a premium for commercial pedigree, what the Oscar Mood's price or sales were, or whether the home line is profitable. Test "Pedigree vs channel messaging price test for a home machine" between T1; T2. Method: Online randomised test: a home-espresso product page (existing Oscar Mood or similar machine, no new hardware) shown to prospective home buyers. Three arms: (a) commercial-pedigree message at a 25% premium over a comparable mass-market home machine, (b) neutral message at the same premium, (c) same pedigree message delivered via a known consumer retailer's storefront. Measure pre-orders or add-to-cart at the displayed price. Ads bought on search and social targeting home-coffee interest.. Sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors per arm (about 9,000 total), recruited through paid search and social ads aimed at home espresso enthusiasts. Estimated, not observed.. Measure: Conversion to a refundable pre-order (or add-to-cart with email capture) per arm, with 95% confidence intervals, plus stated purchase reasons from a short exit survey.. Predictions: T1: Arm (a) converts clearly better than arm (b) at the same price, showing pedigree carries a premium. Arm (c) adds little beyond (a).; T2: Arm (c) converts better than (a), because retailer presence and familiarity drive purchase; pedigree wording alone adds little over (b).. Decision rule: Favour T1 if arm (a) conversion is at least 1.3 times arm (b) with non-overlapping 95% intervals, and arm (c) does not exceed arm (a) by more than 10%. Favour T2 if arm (c) is at least 1.3 times arm (a) with non-overlapping intervals. If neither holds, treat both as unsupported and do not commit capital to either line.. Cost: 14000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a new consumer product line yet. T1 stays open because the Oscar Mood source shows the commercial-component strategy exists, but it gives no price or sales data. New claim: none. Evidence: simo-dcn-oscar-mood-2021.

T2 kept: SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not real data, so I do not cite it. It tests a skill lesson against a product orientation, not consumer-channel reach against pedigree, so it does not bear on T2. T2 stays open: the Breville and Lelit source shows a consumer group bought a prosumer brand, but it does not show why. New claim: none. Evidence: simo-dcn-breville-lelit-2022.

T1 kept: What-if only: if SYN-SIMO-UPDATE were real, its lesson-versus-orientation contrast would bear on learning and hobby engagement, not on whether commercial pedigree earns a price premium. It would change nothing for T1. It is not evidence and will not be cited in finish. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-SIMO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer product line yet. Simonelli already sells a home-oriented machine (the Oscar Mood, built on commercial-derived components), so a pedigree-led home line is the more plausible next step. Before any investment, run the proposed pedigree-versus-channel price test (about 14,000 EUR and 8 weeks, both estimates) to decide between a pedigree-led home product and a channel partnership. If neither result clears the threshold, do not invest in either. Target customer: Home espresso enthusiasts willing to pay a premium for commercial-grade equipment. This segment is inferred from the Oscar Mood and Victoria Arduino E1 Prima positioning and is not sized from data.. Value proposition: Commercial-grade components and professional heritage in a home machine, priced above mass-market home brands. Whether buyers pay that premium is the open question the test is designed to answer.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Design and run the price-and-messaging test (X1), with pre-order conversion across pedigree, neutral and retailer-storefront arms, and check the decision rule before launching. In parallel, look for Oscar Mood sales and margin data, which I could not find in public sources.. Uncertainty: High. I found no independent evidence on whether buyers pay a premium for commercial pedigree. The sources I read were trade-press launch pieces and company product pages, so they show that the strategies exist, not that they pay. The Breville and Lelit source does not show why the acquisition happened. The one synthetic update was not used as evidence. Search coverage was limited to 8 searches, with 6 left unused.. Would change if: The X1 test shows the pedigree arm converting at least 1.3 times the neutral arm at the same premium, with non-overlapping 95% intervals (supports T1); The retailer-storefront arm converts at least 1.3 times the pedigree arm with non-overlapping intervals (supports T2 and a channel partnership); Public or disclosed Oscar Mood sales or margin data show the home line is small or unprofitable, which would argue for no expansion; Evidence that consumer appliance groups buy prosumer brands for product rather than channel reasons would weaken T2; A concrete partner offer to license or distribute, which would make a channel route cheaper to test than building a line. events.text: Objective: Decide whether Aquaporin A/S should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its existing water-membrane offering, and identify the evidence that would justify it. The aim is a sound investment decision, not a predetermined yes.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; company has not asked and has not been contacted; Financial data may be incomplete; state what could not be found; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; 7 searches remain; must read at least three sources; No simulated results may be cited as demand evidence; Must first establish what the company already sells to individual buyers. Alternatives: No expansion: keep selling membranes to OEM and B2B partners only; Product redesign: consumer-facing purifier or cartridge built on existing membranes, sold through current partners; Different route to buyers: license the membrane to established household-appliance or purifier brands (B2B2C); Different customer group: target institutional or emergency/off-grid water buyers rather than households; Specific use-case consumer product (for example a travel or targeted household filter) sold direct-to-consumer; Defer: fund only desk research and a low-cost pre-demand test before committing.
Searched for "Aquaporin consumer water filter product"; found aqp-dwd-recital40-confidence, aqp-flanders-bottled-perceptions, aqp-flint-filters-not-working.
Searched for "Aquaporin Inside membrane"; found aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024, aqp-fy2024-drinking-water-drop.

T1: Households buy point-of-use purifiers mainly to resolve distrust of tap water, so a product that visibly guarantees performance and makes filter replacement effortless can command a price premium and recurring cartridge revenue. Who benefits: Households distrustful of tap water, and the maker that owns the performance guarantee and cartridge relationship. Why behaviour changes: Distrust (taste, safety) is the stated driver of bottled and purchased filtration (Geerts et al., Flanders). Filters fail in use when people do not maintain them (Flint: a health official estimated 50 to 70 percent of filters observed were not working), so a product that removes the maintenance burden and proves it works addresses the real pain.. How value is captured: Aquaporin would need its own brand or a co-brand with a trust-signalling certification and a consumable cartridge sold on subscription, so margin comes from consumables rather than one-off membrane sales.. Assumptions: Purchase intent for purifiers is driven by perceived safety more than by price or design; Consumers will pay a premium for verified performance and automatic replacement reminders; Aquaporin can meet consumer-product certification and customer-service costs without eroding margin; Cartridge replacement rates are high enough to make subscription revenue material. Predictions: In a pre-demand test, households shown a verified-performance claim and auto-replacement show higher stated willingness to pay than households shown a generic filter; Filter-maintenance failure rates fall where replacement is automatic; Sales of purifiers with verified-performance labelling outpace unlabelled models in the same market.

T2: Aquaporin's value in household purifiers is captured mainly by the appliance brand that owns the customer, so a direct consumer product would compete with its own OEM partners and earn less than licensing the membrane into partner brands. Who benefits: Established appliance brands such as Vestel that already own distribution, retail shelf space and customer data. Why behaviour changes: Consumers choose a purifier by brand, store and price, not by which membrane is inside. The brand that sells the product captures the purchase decision, so the membrane supplier's leverage is in being the trusted ingredient, not the retailer.. How value is captured: Aquaporin earns per-unit membrane or licence fees from partner brands, avoiding the marketing, retail and service cost of selling to households itself.. Assumptions: Partner brands have distribution that Aquaporin cannot replicate cheaply; Consumers do not buy purifiers on membrane brand name alone; Partners would see a direct Aquaporin product as channel conflict and reduce orders; Licence economics are more attractive than direct consumer margins after marketing cost. Predictions: Partner brands and retailers are the main point of sale for membrane-based purifiers in Aquaporin's markets; Where Aquaporin has launched under its own name, sales depend on a brand partner rather than on the membrane label; Direct-to-consumer sales of a membrane-branded purifier are small relative to partner volumes in the same market.

T1 supports, from aqp-flanders-bottled-perceptions (independent_study): "For a large part, this is caused by negative perceptions about tap water. Many consumers consider it unhealthy, unsafe and prefer the taste of bottled water.". Does not show: It is about bottled water in Flanders, not purchase of household purifiers, and it does not show that consumers would pay a premium for verified performance or automatic cartridge replacement. Abstract only..

T2 supports, from aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024 (company_assertion): "Turkey's leading technology company, Vestel, has launched a water purifier named Vestel Rafine PRO in cooperation with Aquaporin on its website and in selected stores across Turkey.". Does not show: It is Aquaporin's own press release, so it shows the partner launch but not sales volume, margins or whether a membrane-branded product would sell. It says nothing about channel conflict or licence economics, which T2 also assumes..
Looked for evidence against T2: "Aquaporin direct consumer sales own brand purifier household customers"; found aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-one-purifier-2021, aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse.

T2 contradicts, from aqp-one-purifier-2021 (company_assertion): "With only two cartridges and a replacement indicator on the machine, ONE is easy to install and use. The user friendliness continues, as ONE’s only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.". Does not show: It is the company's own launch claim. It shows Aquaporin already sells a branded purifier through distributors, which cuts against T2's prediction that membrane-branded direct products are absent. It does not show sales volume, margin, or whether the product sells to households or channel conflict arose..

Test "Verified-performance and auto-replacement pre-demand test with a distributor-channel check" between T1; T2. Method: Two-arm online stated-preference survey plus a 4-week landing-page test in one market where the ONE purifier is already distributed. Arm A sees the ONE with a generic filter claim; Arm B sees the same product with a third-party-verified performance claim and automatic cartridge replacement reminders. Separately, record which retailer or distributor page each visitor reaches and whether a membrane-branded direct offer converts differently from a partner-branded offer on the same page.. Sample: Proposed: about 600 respondents for the survey (300 per arm) and about 3,000 unique visitors for the landing page, recruited from a panel in one country (proposed).. Measure: Stated willingness to pay (van Westendorp price points) and pre-order or waitlist sign-up rate by arm; share of sign-ups that choose a membrane-branded versus partner-branded option.. Predictions: T1: Arm B shows at least 15 percent higher stated willingness to pay and higher waitlist sign-up than Arm A; the verified-performance and replacement features drive the difference, not the brand name.; T2: Membrane-branded direct option converts far below the partner-branded option (under half), and the verification premium does not transfer to a direct Aquaporin offer because buyers choose by retailer brand.. Decision rule: Proceed to a consumer-proposition investment only if Arm B exceeds Arm A by at least 15 percent in willingness to pay AND the membrane-branded direct option converts at least 50 percent as well as the partner-branded option. If the first holds but the second fails, pursue a licensed or co-branded verified-performance product through partners (T1 via T2's channel). If neither holds, do not invest beyond desk research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.
Looked for evidence against T1: "tap water trust purifier filter premium willingness to pay household"; found aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse, aqp-flint-filters-not-working, aqp-eurostat-household-use.

T1 supports, from aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse (independent_study): "At the time of survey, 24% of households (107/452) did not use filters; the most common reason given was breakage (42%).". Does not show: Filters here were donated to tsunami-affected households, not bought, so it says nothing about willingness to pay or premium for verified performance. It supports only the claim that filters go unused and fail, which makes maintenance and replacement a real pain point. Abstract only..

Favours T1: Do not commit to a standalone direct-to-consumer launch yet. Run the proposed X1 test, which compares a verified-performance and automatic-replacement offer against a generic one and checks whether a membrane-branded direct offer converts as well as a partner-branded one. If X1 supports T1, pursue a verified-performance, replacement-led product through partners, with Aquaporin capturing consumable and licence value. If neither holds, keep to B2B and partner licensing and fund no further consumer work. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: SYN-AQP-UPDATE is simulated, so I do not use it as evidence. T1 stays an untested hypothesis. Read evidence still supports only that tap-water distrust drives bottled-water choice and that filters go unused or break. Neither shows a purchase premium for verified performance, so X1 is still needed. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-flanders-bottled-perceptions; aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse.

T2 revised: Aquaporin's own ONE launch shows it already sells a branded purifier through distributors, which cuts against T2's claim that a membrane-branded direct product would be absent or sit in channel conflict. The Vestel launch still shows partners carry membrane products to market. Both are company claims and say nothing about volumes or margins, so T2 is weakened, not rejected. New claim: Aquaporin captures value mainly through partner brands and distributors, but it already runs a branded product through distributors, so a direct or co-branded offer is possible and its economics are unknown.. Evidence: aqp-one-purifier-2021; aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024.

T1 kept: The simulated update is excluded from evidence, so T1 is unchanged. It remains untested. The read evidence on distrust and unused or broken filters supports the pain point but not a verified-performance premium. X1 is still required. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-flint-filters-not-working; aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse.

T1 kept: What-if only: if SYN-AQP-UPDATE were real, it would bear on T1 solely as enrollment in a maintenance plan under an assumed legal supply route. It would not show a verified-performance premium, correct long-term use, market size or company funding. It changes nothing; I do not count it as evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-AQP-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a standalone direct-to-consumer launch now. Keep the core business in B2B and partner licensing. Before any consumer investment, run the proposed X1 test (proposed cost 18,000 EUR, 10 weeks, within the 20,000 EUR and 12-week limits). Only if X1 supports T1 should Aquaporin consider a verified-performance, replacement-led product through partners, with value captured in consumables and licences. Target customer: Households that already use or are considering a point-of-use purifier and distrust tap water, reached through partner brands and retailers in markets where Aquaporin already has distribution.. Value proposition: Verified performance and automatic cartridge replacement that addresses the maintenance failures that leave filters unused. This is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated premium.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Request financial statements and partner sales data, since public sources give only company press-release figures. Then design X1 with a partner in one market and apply the threshold: proceed only if the verified-performance arm beats the generic arm by at least 15 percent on willingness to pay, and the membrane-branded direct offer converts at least 50 percent as well as the partner-branded one.. Uncertainty: High. No independent data on Aquaporin's channel revenue, margins, cash or financing. Only company press-release figures: FY2024 Drinking Water revenue down 55% to DKK 18 million (key-account demand change); Industrial Water up 192% to DKK 10.5 million. Simulated update not used as evidence. Sources: 5 read items, several abstract-only. No evidence measures household willingness to pay for verified performance. The 2021 ONE launch shows a branded purifier already sold through distributors, which weakens T2 and is unresolved.. Would change if: X1 shows no premium for verified performance or auto-replacement, rejecting T1 and pointing to B2B-only; The membrane-branded direct offer converts well below the partner-branded offer, supporting T2 and ruling out a direct product; Financial statements show weak cash or funding capacity, making consumer investment unaffordable regardless of demand; Partner sales data show household demand driven by brand and retail channel rather than membrane or performance claims; Independent data show households do not maintain or replace cartridges, undermining the subscription revenue assumption. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; company not contacted and its intentions unknown; Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Company financial data may be incomplete; state what could not be found; Company assertions are not proof of demand; Do not cite SIMULATED results in finish. Alternatives: A: No expansion, keep supplying membranes to OEM and industrial partners only; B: Product redesign, a consumer-branded purifier or cartridge for one defined use case; C: Different route to buyers, such as retailers, partners or subscriptions, without owning a finished device; D: Different customer group, such as small commercial, hospitality, off-grid or humanitarian users; E: Licensing or component supply to existing consumer purifier brands, keeping consumer risk off the balance sheet; F: Staged option, a low-cost demand test in one use case before any build.

T1: Aquaporin captures most value by supplying its membrane as an ingredient inside brand-owned purifiers, because household buyers choose a purifier on brand, design and price, not on the membrane, so a partner's distribution and trust earns more than a standalone Aquaporin consumer product would. Who benefits: Aquaporin (supply revenue per unit and cartridge refills) and the partner brand (Philips, Vestel) who owns the customer relationship. Why behaviour changes: Household buyers judge a purifier by brand trust, retail presence and price; a recognised brand carrying an Aquaporin-powered label adds credibility without Aquaporin needing its own consumer marketing or retail.. How value is captured: Exclusive or regional supply agreements paid per membrane or per cartridge, with recurring replacement volume tied to the partner's installed base. Assumptions: Partner brands value a differentiating membrane enough to pay a premium; Consumers would not pay materially more for a membrane brand name alone; Exclusivity agreements persist long enough to earn back supply investment. Predictions: Partner-branded units sell through at materially higher volume than any Aquaporin-only branded unit would; Aquaporin revenue growth is concentrated in a small number of partner contracts; Consumer marketing of the membrane brand is minimal in partner product literature.

T2: Consumers in the target market will pay a premium for a purifier whose health benefit is visible and specific (for example, removal of a named contaminant), so a differentiated use-case product sold under Aquaporin's own name can earn a price premium over generic purifiers. Who benefits: Aquaporin, if it owns the product and the claimed benefit is credible; and households worried about a specific contaminant. Why behaviour changes: A concrete, verifiable benefit for a felt risk makes the purchase feel necessary rather than discretionary, which reduces price sensitivity relative to a generic 'clean water' claim.. How value is captured: Higher unit price and margin on a branded device or cartridge subscription, provided the benefit is certified and the buyer can see it. Assumptions: The target households have a specific, recognised contaminant concern; Independent certification of the benefit is available and affordable; Buyers accept a higher price for the claimed benefit. Predictions: Stated willingness to pay is higher for a product naming a specific contaminant than for a generic purifier; Purchases concentrate in areas with a known local contaminant problem; Premium holds only where the benefit is independently certified.

Exclusivity terms and the share of revenue from this contract are not stated..

Any interest in the membrane technology should first establish the asset, IP and partner-contract position through the trustee. A standalone consumer brand is not supported by the public evidence. The partner-supply model is the better-supported route, but the evidence for it is company claims only. Target customer: None identified for Aquaporin. Partner brands (Philips in China, Vestel in Turkey) are the buyers the public evidence points to, not individual households.. Value proposition: Membrane supply to partner-branded purifiers, earning per-unit and cartridge revenue, rather than a self-branded consumer device.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Check the bankruptcy file and trustee sale process for asset, IP and contract status. Confirm whether the Philips and Vestel supply agreements are still active and who holds them. No consumer test is recommended until ownership is clear.. Uncertainty: Financial data is incomplete: no revenue split, contract values, exclusivity terms, unit volumes or margins were found. The 95% growth and the doubling of Philips China sales are company assertions. The Vestel launch confirms a product exists but not its sales. The only independent item is a 2012 Sri Lanka abstract on ceramic filter disuse, which is an analogy and not a membrane consumer study. Consumer purchase drivers for membrane purifiers are unmeasured. Company status after the bankruptcy is confirmed only by the court order.. Would change if: The trustee confirms the IP and partner contracts are sold to a buyer who can operate them, and that buyer asks for a demand test; Independent data shows partner-branded membrane purifiers selling well with the membrane brand not visible to buyers; Independent evidence shows households pay a measurable premium for a named, certified contaminant benefit; Partner contracts are shown to be a small share of past revenue, making the partner route less important. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Premium vs Simplicity Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from self-identified home baristas (n=300). Participants view a product description of a Simonelli consumer model (e.g., Eagle One Prima) and are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) Premium design and status messaging; (B) Simplicity and ease of use messaging. After viewing the description, participants indicate their likelihood to purchase the product on a 7‑point scale (1‑Very unlikely, 7‑Very likely) and state their top purchase reason (design/brand, ease of use, or other).. Sample: 300 self‑identified home baristas recruited via coffee forums and social media, balanced across messaging conditions.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑to 7) and top purchase reason for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5 and ease of use will rank as the top reason for ≥ 30% of respondents.; T2: Condition B will achieve a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5 and simplicity will rank as the top reason for ≥ 30% of respondents.. Decision rule: If Condition A’s mean purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and ease of use is the top reason for ≥ 30% of respondents, proceed to develop a premium‑design consumer proposition. If Condition B’s mean purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and simplicity is the top reason for ≥ 30% of respondents, develop a simplicity‑focused consumer proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and maintain the current portfolio.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Sample: Proposed: about 1,500 German home-cook visitors recruited via paid social and a cooking-enthusiast panel, filtered for owning a built-in or countertop oven; plus five to eight appliance-maker contacts found from the public list of combi-steamer makers.. Measure: Pre-order or refundable deposit conversion rate in the branded arm versus a neutral-brand control at the same price; number of appliance makers that agree to a formal licence discussion within the window.. Predictions: T1: Branded conversion clearly above the neutral-brand control at the same price, and a price point that clears unit cost; partners show little interest because the brand is the asset.; T2: Branded conversion no better than the neutral control, and at least two appliance makers request a formal licence or supply discussion.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: if branded deposit conversion is at least 1.5 times the neutral control and at least 2 percent overall, continue T1 and build a branded home prototype. If at least two appliance makers request a licence discussion and branded conversion is not above the control, favour T2 and pursue a partner route. If neither holds, decline further home expansion and stay professional.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not start a RATIONAL-branded home product yet. Keep the professional focus, and test a partner route (supply or licence of steaming technology to home-appliance makers) before committing capital to a consumer brand. The public evidence I read does not show home-cook demand for a RATIONAL product, and the main sources are a company estimate of total market potential and a sous-vide acquisition that is a different product. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not start a RATIONAL-branded home product now. Keep the professional focus as the base case, and run a low-cost test of a partner route (supply or licence of steaming technology to home-appliance makers) before committing capital to a consumer brand. The public evidence I read does not show home-cook demand for a RATIONAL product. Target customer: Professional kitchens remain the target. Home cooks are a possible later segment, reached first through appliance makers that already own the consumer channel.. Value proposition: For professional buyers, the existing combi-steamer proposition is unchanged. For a possible partner, RATIONAL's steaming technology would be offered as a component or licence that the partner brands and sells to home cooks.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Run the proposed partner-interest probe (concept test X1, about 18,000 EUR and 12 weeks; both figures are my proposals, not company figures): approach five to eight home-appliance makers for a formal licence discussion, with a small branded pre-order concept test as the control arm. Decide using the threshold in the proposed decision rule.. Uncertainty: High. I did not verify whether RATIONAL already sells to individual buyers, and my searches did not produce its financial data, so I cannot say how large any home business is or reconcile its revenue split. The 4.8 million potential customers is a company estimate of total market, not home demand, and does not separate home cooks. The Anova acquisition concerns a different sous-vide product. The test figures and thresholds are my proposals. No test has been run, and nothing I found measures willingness to pay for a combi-steamer in a home.. Would change if: Company or regulatory filings show RATIONAL already sells a significant volume to home buyers, which would change the starting point for any home proposition; Concept test shows branded pre-order conversion at least 1.5 times a neutral-brand control and at least 2 percent overall, which would favour T1 and a branded home prototype; Appliance makers decline licence talks while branded interest is weak, which would point to staying professional; Evidence shows home buyers cannot fit a professional-size unit in a kitchen, which would weaken both home routes. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Households buy laundry machines as a utility purchase on price and space, so a commercial-grade machine adapted for home use would not win a premium with individual buyers; value is captured only where a third party operates the machine for many users. Who benefits: Multi-family building owners, student housing operators and campsites that run shared machines for residents or guests. Why behaviour changes: The operator wants uptime, serviceability and return on investment for shared machines, and residents pay per use rather than buying their own. How value is captured: EPG sells commercial machines and service to the operator, who earns revenue from resident use. Assumptions: Residents in shared buildings have no own machine and pay per cycle; Operators buy on total cost of ownership and uptime; Individual households do not pay a premium for commercial durability. Predictions: Operator-run formats keep growing in multi-family and student housing where residents lack in-unit machines; Consumer-grade products adapted from commercial machines show weak take-up in household surveys or retail sales; EPG's consumer-operated offers are described on operator-facing pages rather than with household product launches.

T2: Individual households value laundry as a convenience they will pay for only when home space or time is the binding constraint, so a compact, lower-capacity version of a commercial machine sold directly to small-space households could earn a premium over standard consumer machines. Who benefits: Renters and urban households in small homes or flats with no space for a full-size machine, and the manufacturer if it can sell at a premium. Why behaviour changes: Space and time scarcity make a compact, durable, fast machine worth more than a standard household model. How value is captured: EPG sells a redesigned compact unit through consumer retail or online channels at a price above standard household machines. Assumptions: Small-space households have unmet demand for a durable compact laundry machine; Buyers will pay a premium for durability and speed; EPG can reach these buyers through existing channels at acceptable cost. Predictions: Compact-laundry searches and listings grow in urban housing markets; Households in small spaces report laundry as a pain point in surveys; A priced test offer converts at a rate above a set threshold.

Does not show: It does not show that households or residents buy their own machines, that individual buyers pay a premium, or how many consumer-operated sites exist or sell..

Test "Segment pre-order test: small-space households vs shared-site operators" between T1; T2. Method: Run two paid-search and social landing pages at the same time. One targets households in small urban flats and offers a refundable deposit on a compact commercial-grade machine. The other targets operators of student housing, short-let and campsite laundry and offers a quote request for a shared-use unit. Price points shown are proposed and the deposit is refundable.. Sample: Proposed: about 4,000 qualified ad clicks per arm over 6 weeks, with an estimated 800 to 1,000 operator-side contacts from trade channels. Measure: Deposit or quote-request conversion rate per 100 qualified visitors, and the price at which buyers abandon. Predictions: T1: Operator-side quote requests convert clearly higher than household deposits, and household deposits stay near zero at the tested premium; T2: Small-space household deposits convert at a meaningful rate at a premium over standard machines, and operator conversion is no better than household conversion. Decision rule: Proposed: continue on T2 only if small-space households convert at 2 or more deposits per 100 qualified visitors at a premium of at least 20 percent over a standard machine. Favour T1 if operator quote conversion is at least 2 times household conversion and household conversion is below 1 per 100. Otherwise stop and do not invest.. Cost: 14000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a consumer product yet. Keep the professional and shared-site offer. Run the proposed segment test (X1) before any consumer product spend, because the evidence read so far is company-authored and shows only that EPG already serves consumer-operated shared laundry, not that households would pay a premium for a compact machine. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: No real evidence has been added since the position was stated. The simulated item SYN-EPRO-UPDATE is not cited and does not change my view. T1 stays as it was: the evidence is company-authored and shows that EPG serves consumer-operated shared laundry. T2 kept: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE is labelled SIMULATED and is a hypothetical case-author construction, so it is not real evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer product now. Keep the professional and shared-site offer, and run a low-cost segment test before any consumer spend. Target customer: Not chosen. Shared-site operators (student housing, short-let, campsites) are the better-evidenced group. Small-space households are a hypothesis still to test.. Value proposition: For shared-site operators: reliability, serviceability and uptime for multi-user machines, as EPG's own pages describe. For households: not yet established.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run test X1 (proposed, EUR 14,000, 8 weeks, within the EUR 20,000 and 12-week limits), comparing household deposits with operator quote requests, and apply its decision rule. Also look for EPG's consumer-operated sales and retail channel data, which I could not find in public sources.. Uncertainty: High. All EPG sources are company-authored, undated product or corporate pages with no sales figures. I found no public data on EPG's consumer or consumer-operated revenue, no household demand or price-premium study, and no financial or contractual detail on partnerships or licensing. The Which? piece is from 2020 and about sustainability, not commercial-grade premiums. Speed Queen's claim is a rival's marketing, not evidence of sales. Test X1 is only proposed and nothing has been run.. Would change if: X1 shows small-space households converting at 2 or more deposits per 100 qualified visitors at a 20% or higher premium over a standard machine (proposed threshold); EPG's public or company-provided figures show material existing sales to individual households through retail or online channels; Independent data show rising small-space or urban demand for durable compact laundry, with willingness to pay; A licensing or partnership counterparty offers a funded consumer route that needs no EPG consumer distribution. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Home cooks will purchase a differentiated combi-steamer only if it is marketed as a premium, lifestyle cooking tool that offers superior health benefits (e.g., steam-cooking savings) and design appeal, because they currently view combi-steamers as industrial equipment and prefer established consumer brands. Who benefits: Health-conscious home cooks willing to pay a premium for convenience and health advantages.. Why behaviour changes: If RATIONAL frames the product as a modern, stylish appliance that delivers faster, healthier meals, they will shift from generic appliances to a premium offering.. How value is captured: Higher price points and repeat purchases from a niche segment of affluent home cooks.. Assumptions: Home cooks perceive steam-cooking as a benefit.; There is a segment willing to pay a premium for design and convenience.; Marketing can differentiate RATIONAL's technology from competitors.. Predictions: A survey of home cooks would show at least 30% would consider purchasing a premium combi-steamer at a price 20% above standard models.; Sales would be concentrated among demographics with higher disposable income and interest in culinary gadgets..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer primarily because of convenience and time savings, not premium design or health benefits, because they already use multiple appliances and seek solutions that reduce cooking time. Who benefits: Busy home cooks who value efficiency and time savings in meal preparation.. Why behaviour changes: If RATIONAL offers a compact, single-appliance solution that cooks multiple dishes simultaneously, home cooks will switch from a collection of separate appliances to a streamlined system.. How value is captured: Higher volume sales through a single product and repeat purchases due to convenience.. Assumptions: Home cooks have limited cooking time and prefer one appliance for multiple tasks.; Time savings are a primary purchase driver for home cooks.; RATIONAL can demonstrate measurable time savings in product testing.. Predictions: A pilot test of a compact combi-steamer would show at least 40% of participants reducing cooking time by at least 30 minutes per meal.; Purchase intent would be higher among households with children or multiple meals to prepare daily..

Test "Home Cook Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and a simulated purchase decision.. Sample: 500 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income.. case.question: Should Aquaporin A/S develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing water-membrane offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

Table 2 presents households' water use from public supply. It varies across European countries - the median is around 40-50 cubic metres per inhabitant and has been decreasing slightly over the last few decades.

With only two cartridges and a replacement indicator on the machine, ONE is easy to install and use. The user friendliness continues, as ONE’s only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.

Signed an exclusive supply agreement with AquaShield, the global brand partner of Philips Water Solutions for supply of membrane to all Philips-branded purifiers in China, with a doubling of sales compared to 2022

Turkey's leading technology company, Vestel, has launched a water purifier named Vestel Rafine PRO in cooperation with Aquaporin on its website and in selected stores across Turkey. The Aquaporin Inside® technology powers the Vestel Rafine PRO water purifier.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Aquaporin A/S should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing water-membrane offering, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst; public sources only; company not contacted and its intentions unknown; Financial data may be incomplete; report what could not be found; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; 7 searches remaining, so searches must be targeted; Must first establish how far the company already reaches individual buyers. Alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B or OEM membrane supplier and invest nothing in consumer-facing work; Product redesign: build a consumer-ready household purifier or cartridge around existing membranes; Different route to buyers: supply or license membranes to existing consumer purifier brands rather than sell a branded product; Different customer group: target institutional, humanitarian, hospitality or off-grid buyers instead of mainstream households; Narrow pilot: test one specific consumer use case, such as premium drinking-water filtration or portable purification, before full commitment; Licensing the biomimetic technology into a non-water consumer category.
Searched for "Aquaporin consumer water purifier product"; found aqp-one-purifier-2021, aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024.

T1: Consumers choose a household purifier partly because of a visible technology credential ('Aquaporin Inside'), so a branded ingredient supplier earns a supply premium or royalty from partner brands without needing its own retail presence. Who benefits: Aquaporin (ingredient-brand royalties and exclusive supply) and partner brands that gain a differentiating credential. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who cannot judge membrane performance use a named technology badge as a proxy for filtration quality and safety, and are willing to pay more for it.. How value is captured: Exclusive or multi-year supply agreements per region (e.g., Philips China, Vestel Turkey) priced per membrane or cartridge, plus co-marketing that carries the Aquaporin name.. Assumptions: Buyers notice and respond to a named component badge at the point of purchase; Partner brands pay a price premium over an unbranded membrane that covers Aquaporin's cost; Exclusivity limits rivals from supplying the same partner brand in that region. Predictions: Partner-brand purifiers that display the Aquaporin badge sell at a measurable price premium over otherwise identical models without it; Aquaporin's revenue from partner supply grows with the number of partner-branded SKUs rather than with direct consumer sales; Where the badge is removed or not displayed, partner sales volume falls relative to comparable models.

T2: Value in household purifiers comes mainly from recurring cartridge replacement, not from the device. A manufacturer that controls the cartridge membrane and its replacement schedule can earn a steady margin per household, even if device prices are low or the brand is weak. Who benefits: Aquaporin, if it supplies or owns the replaceable cartridge; device makers gain the device sale but depend on the cartridge supplier.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers buy a purifier once and then re-buy cartridges on a schedule or when an indicator tells them to. Their repeat purchases follow the cartridge, not the appliance brand, so the supplier of a proprietary cartridge gets repeat revenue.. How value is captured: Per-cartridge price with the replacement indicator tied to the membrane, possibly with a proprietary cartridge format; revenue scales with installed base and replacement frequency.. Assumptions: Cartridge replacement is needed on a predictable schedule and consumers do not refill or substitute cheap cartridges; Proprietary or indicator-linked cartridge format is hard for rivals to copy; Installed base grows through partner devices or own devices. Predictions: Partner or own purifiers using the Aquaporin cartridge show a higher share of replacement-cartridge sales than purifiers using generic cartridges; Cartridge revenue per installed unit stays stable over several years; If cartridge formats are opened to third-party cartridges, price per cartridge falls and Aquaporin's margin shrinks.

T1 neutral, from aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024 (company_assertion): "The Aquaporin Inside® technology powers the Vestel Rafine PRO water purifier.". Does not show: Shows that Aquaporin is named on the Vestel product and in a partnership, but not that the badge affects buyer choice, price premium, or sales. It is a company press release with no sales or price data..

T2 supports, from aqp-philips-china-supply-2023 (company_assertion): "Signed an exclusive supply agreement with AquaShield, the global brand partner of Philips Water Solutions for supply of membrane to all Philips-branded purifiers in China, with a doubling of sales compared to 2022". Does not show: Shows that Aquaporin supplies membranes to Philips-branded purifiers under an exclusive deal and that its sales doubled. It does not show that the supply is priced per cartridge, that replacement cartridges recur, or that the cartridge format is proprietary. It is a company bullet point, not an audited breakdown..

Looked for evidence against T2: "cartridge replacement third-party cartridges price per cartridge purifier membrane"; found aqp-one-purifier-2021, aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-eurostat-household-use.

Test "Badge premium and cartridge economics check in one partner market" between T1; T2. Method: Two-part desk and survey study. (a) Price-scrape purifiers in Turkey from the Vestel Rafine PRO line and comparable models with no named membrane supplier, recording device price, cartridge price, and replacement interval as stated by the maker. (b) Online discrete-choice survey of household buyers in the same market, where respondents pick between otherwise identical purifiers with and without the 'Aquaporin Inside' badge and with different cartridge prices.. Sample: About 300 adults who have bought or plan to buy a countertop or tap purifier in the last 12 months (proposed size, estimated for a choice experiment with 3 to 4 attributes). Measure: Willingness to pay for the badge (EUR per device); share of choices driven by badge versus cartridge price; cartridge price and replacement interval across badged and unbadged models. Predictions: T1: Badged models carry a measurable price or choice premium over identical unbadged models, and the premium is large enough to cover the supplier's per-unit royalty.; T2: Badge has little effect on choice; cartridge price and replacement interval drive the lifetime cost, and badged models use a proprietary cartridge with a higher share of lifetime spend going to cartridges.. Decision rule: Keep T1 if badge premium is at least 10% of device price in the choice model with a 95% interval excluding zero. Keep T2 if badge coefficient is not distinguishable from zero and cartridge price explains at least twice the choice weight of badge. If neither holds, drop both and treat the consumer proposition as unproven.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not commit to a branded consumer product yet. Aquaporin already reaches individual buyers through partner brands (Philips China, Vestel Turkey) and a distributor-sold ONE purifier. Before any consumer investment, test whether the recurring cartridge economics that partner supply implies are real, and whether a visible badge adds value. Keep the partner-supply route as the default and treat a branded consumer proposition as unproven. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T2 kept: SYN-AQP-UPDATE is SIMULATED, so it is not evidence and T2 is unchanged by it. The real evidence I read still supports T2 only weakly: the Philips China exclusive supply deal is company-stated and says nothing about cartridge pricing or replacement cycles. Still untested. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-philips-china-supply-2023.

T2 kept: What-if only: SYN-AQP-UPDATE is SIMULATED, not real demand. If it were real, a scheduled-delivery plan enrolling 120 of 400 households versus 60 of 400 in the self-service arm would point toward recurring maintenance driving uptake, which fits T2. Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Lifestyle Condition (premium design, social-sharing features) or Convenience Condition (compact, easy-to-use machine). Both conditions present the same Simonelli consumer product concept at a fixed price point. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across Lifestyle and Convenience conditions to test both hypotheses.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for the differentiated Simonelli consumer product.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price in the Lifestyle Condition compared to the Convenience Condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price in the Convenience Condition compared to the Lifestyle Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in the Lifestyle Condition is at least 5 points higher than in the Convenience Condition (i.e., Lifestyle ≥ Convenience + 5 points), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on lifestyle/social sharing. events.text: Objective: Decide whether Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific home or prosumer use case, beyond its professional espresso-equipment offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only, with no company contact or internal data; Company financials may not be fully public, so gaps must be stated; Test budget assumed at EUR 20000 and 12 weeks maximum (analyst assumptions, not company figures); 8 searches in total, 7 remaining after the brief, with one challenge_theory search kept for falsification; Company claims must not be treated as proof of consumer demand. Alternatives: No expansion: remain professional-only under the Nuova Simonelli and Victoria Arduino commercial focus; Product redesign: a scaled-down or home-oriented version of existing commercial machines sold under existing brands; Different route to buyers: sell prosumer machines online or through retail, or via existing café-equipment dealers serving enthusiasts; Different customer group: target home baristas or small-office prosumers with a dedicated line, or adjacent grinders and accessories only; Licensing or partnership with an established home-appliance maker to reach consumer distribution without owning the consumer brand; Acquisition of an established home-espresso brand.

T1: Home and prosumer espresso buyers will pay a premium for commercial-grade components and build quality from a manufacturer with a professional heritage, so a Simonelli-branded prosumer line sold through enthusiast channels can earn premium margins. Who benefits: Home and prosumer enthusiasts who want café-grade performance, and Simonelli, which would earn premium margins on existing component and manufacturing capability.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers of high-end home espresso treat the machine as a long-term purchase and a status signal. A professional pedigree reduces their perceived risk and justifies a higher price than comparable consumer machines.. How value is captured: Simonelli sells a higher-priced home or prosumer model under its own brand through specialist dealers or online, keeping the margin that a consumer brand would otherwise need to pay to a third party.. Assumptions: Enthusiasts value commercial components enough to pay a clear premium over well-regarded prosumer machines; Simonelli can reach these buyers through dealers or online channels without a large consumer marketing budget; The Oscar line already gives the company a credible home-facing product to build on. Predictions: Oscar-type home models sell at a measurable price premium over comparable prosumer machines from non-professional brands; Enthusiast reviews and forum discussions cite professional components or pedigree as a reason for purchase; A limited launch through specialist dealers sells through at a target price without heavy discounting.

T2: Home espresso demand is won by brands with consumer distribution and marketing reach, not by component pedigree, so a professional manufacturer captures little value from a home line unless it buys or partners with a consumer brand. Who benefits: Consumer-focused brands with retail and marketing reach, such as Breville, which can convert the same engineering into premium sales through their own channels.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers choose a home machine on brand familiarity, retail availability, warranty and marketing rather than on the origin of its boiler or pump, so a manufacturer without consumer reach struggles to convert pedigree into sales.. How value is captured: The consumer brand owner earns the retail margin and brand premium. A professional manufacturer earns only component or OEM margin, or the value of a sale to the acquirer.. Assumptions: Consumer purchase decisions are driven more by brand and distribution than by professional heritage; Professional manufacturers lack the marketing and retail reach to win these buyers alone; Consolidation in the prosumer segment means consumer brands with reach are the main beneficiaries. Predictions: Prosumer machines from brands with strong retail distribution outsell pedigree-only brands at similar prices; Simonelli's home-facing sales, if any, stay small without a retail partner; Acquisitions of prosumer brands are priced on distribution and brand assets rather than engineering pedigree.

T1 supports, from simo-dcn-oscar-mood-2021 (market_fact): "The Oscar Mood is the successor in the line to the Oscar II, and the original Nuova Simonelli Oscar, which introduced some of Nuova Simonelli’s high-quality and high-powered components to high-end home and prosumer audiences.". Does not show: It shows that a home-facing line already exists, not that buyers pay a premium for professional components, how many units sell, or at what margin. The description of the components is the manufacturer's own framing, relayed by a trade outlet..

It says nothing about whether distribution or marketing, rather than component pedigree, drives purchase, and the article gives no buyer-level data.
